slides.direction: 🔴 DANGEROUS: `git stash drop`. What it changes: one log line is removed and `refs/stash` moves or is deleted. What it can destroy: the only name of that entry. Preview: `git stash show -p` on the entry. Recovery: by the ID that `drop` prints, while the objects exist. Appropriate: for an entry you have applied or no longer need.

slides.body: Five mistakes to watch for. Almost everyone makes the first one.

items: Expecting git stash pop to restore what was staged. Root cause: apply and pop merge W with H as the base; only --index also reads I, the second parent.
Reading git stash show -p as "what I had unstaged". Root cause: it is the diff from H to W, so the staged and unstaged parts appear as one change.
Treating a dropped stash as deleted. Root cause: drop removes a reflog line; the commits stay in the object database, unreachable, until a prune.
Expecting stashes on another machine after a push. Root cause: nothing fetches or pushes refs/stash; export and import exist since Git 2.51 for that purpose.
Searching for a stash by the message shown in the list. Root cause: the list prints the reflog message, which can differ from the commit's subject.

slides.lead: Let's land this. You should now be able to say:
items: A stash entry is a merge commit W with parents H and I, and a third parentless parent U when untracked files are included.
The staged change is the difference between H and I; the unstaged change is the difference between I and W.
refs/stash names the newest entry and the stash list is that ref's reflog.
git stash create builds an entry without touching anything, and git stash store lists an existing one.
A dropped entry is still a commit; with its ID I can store or apply it until it is pruned.

slides.body: Today you opened a stash entry and found ordinary commits inside.

beats.text: She had spent twenty minutes with git add -p, staging exactly the hunks, the blocks of changed lines, that belonged in the next commit, and leaving the debugging lines unstaged. Then an interruption, git stash, which parks uncommitted work and resets the files. A branch switch, and later git stash pop. Every change came back as unstaged. The separation she had built is gone from git status.
beats.tele: She had spent twenty minutes with `git add -p`, staging exactly the hunks, the blocks of changed lines, that belonged in the next commit, and leaving the debugging lines unstaged. Then an interruption, `git stash`, which parks uncommitted work and resets the files. A branch switch, and later `git stash pop`. Every change came back as unstaged. The separation she had built is gone from `git status`.

beats.text: The short answer for the CTO is: nothing was lost. A stash entry is a commit with two or three parents, and the second parent holds the index, the staging area, as it was. A plain git stash pop ignores it. And pop printed the ID of the commit it dropped.

beats.text: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. You learned the stash commands in the undo module: push, list, apply, pop, drop. In the recovery module you rescued a dropped entry by treating it as an unreachable merge commit. Today you open one up.
beats.tele: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. You learned the stash commands in the undo module: push, list, apply, pop, drop. In the recovery module you rescued a dropped entry by treating it as an unreachable merge commit. Today you open one up.

beats.text: This chapter has a theme that will come back in every video of this module. A repository holds content that is versioned and travels with clone, fetch and push. And it holds machinery that is local and never travels: .git/config, .git/hooks, .git/rr-cache, refs/stash. The stash is on the local side of that line.
beats.tele: This chapter has a theme that will come back in every video of this module. A repository holds content that is versioned and travels with clone, fetch and push. And it holds machinery that is local and never travels: `.git/config`, `.git/hooks`, `.git/rr-cache`, `refs/stash`. The stash is on the local side of that line.

beats.text: In one sentence: a stash entry is a commit W that records your tracked files. Its first parent is H, the commit that was HEAD. Its second parent is a commit I that records the index. And when you stash untracked files, a parentless commit U is its third. A parent is the commit another commit was built on.
beats.tele: In one sentence: a stash entry is a commit W that records your tracked files. Its first parent is H, the commit that was HEAD. Its second parent is a commit I that records the index. And when you stash untracked files, a parentless commit U is its third. A parent is the commit another commit was built on.

beats.text: refs/stash points at the newest W, and the stash list is the reflog of that ref: the local list of values the ref has had.
beats.tele: `refs/stash` points at the newest W, and the stash list is the reflog of that ref: the local list of values the ref has had.

beats.text: Precisely, in the manual's words: W is "a commit whose tree records the state of the working directory", its first parent is the commit at HEAD, and "the tree of the second parent records the state of the index". The manual doesn't name the third parent. git stash show --include-untracked and --only-untracked read it.
beats.tele: Precisely, in the manual's words: W is "a commit whose tree records the state of the working directory", its first parent is the commit at HEAD, and "the tree of the second parent records the state of the index". The manual doesn't name the third parent. `git stash show --include-untracked` and `--only-untracked` read it.

beats.text: Revision syntax works on an entry. stash@{1}^2 is the index commit of the second entry. stash@{0}:config.yaml is one file of the newest. And stash@{n} is reflog syntax. There is one ref.

beats.text: Inside the dot git folder: new objects for W, I and, with -u or -a, U. The ref refs/stash. And the log logs/refs/stash, one line per entry.

beats.text: Two plumbing subcommands split push into its halves. git stash create builds the commits and prints the ID of W. No ref is written and the files stay as they are. git stash store puts an existing stash commit on the list. Scripts use them, and so does Git: the autostash of git rebase --autostash is a stash commit that is never put on the list.

Scripts use them, and so does Git: the autostash of `git rebase --autostash` is a stash commit that is never put on the list.

beats.text: What drop does: it deletes one line from the log and adjusts the ref. No object is deleted. The commit is unreachable until unreachable objects are pruned, two weeks by default.
beats.tele: What `drop` does: it deletes one line from the log and adjusts the ref. No object is deleted. The commit is unreachable until unreachable objects are pruned, two weeks by default.

beats.text: And travel: nothing fetches or pushes refs/stash. Since Git 2.51, git stash export writes all entries into one chain of ordinary commits that can be pushed like a branch, and git stash import turns such a chain back into entries.
beats.tele: And travel: nothing fetches or pushes `refs/stash`. Since Git 2.51, `git stash export` writes all entries into one chain of ordinary commits that can be pushed like a branch, and `git stash import` turns such a chain back into entries.

beats.text: When not to stash: for anything long-lived. You saw in the recovery module that only the newest entry is held by a ref. Long-lived work belongs on a branch.
beats.tele: When not to stash: for anything long-lived. You saw in the recovery module that only the newest entry is held by a ref. Long-lived work belongs on a branch.

beats.text: The textbook's analogy: a labelled envelope with two or three sheets. A photocopy of the bench, which is the files. A photocopy of the outbox, which is the index. And the loose notes that were lying around, the untracked files.

beats.text: The analogy breaks in one place: there is no drawer for the envelopes. They are ordinary commits in the object database, held by one ref and its log. That's why a dropped stash can be found again, and also why an expired log loses the list.
